Walyson, thank you for the farm visit. Can I ask you about prices? This system is new for me.
Of course. Most arabica is priced on the futures market, which is in New York.
So the price that I see on the screen is the final price?
Not exactly. That's the base. Then we add a differential, which depends on the quality and the origin.
I see. And who decides the differential?
We negotiate it with the buyer. Sometimes a broker, who connects buyers and sellers, helps us.
And how do you check the quality of a lot?
First we look at the green coffee for defects and check the moisture content. Then we do a cupping.

Every morning, the first thing that a coffee trader checks is the futures market in New York. The futures price is the base price for arabica coffee around the world, and it changes every minute. But nobody pays only the futures price. The real price of a lot is the futures price plus a differential, which depends on the quality, the origin and the market. Then there is the spot price, which is the price for coffee that you can deliver now. Why is all this important? Because prices can go up or down very fast. A frost in Brazil can change everything in one night. That is why companies hedge. A roaster that buys coffee for next year can fix part of the price today, so a big change in the market does not destroy its budget. My advice for new traders is simple: learn the words first. If you understand the futures, the differential and the hedge, you understand the business.

I have been working as a coffee taster in Santos for twelve years. My day starts at seven, when the samples that arrived the day before are ready. First, I look at the green coffee. I count the defects, the black and broken beans that lower the quality. Then I check the moisture content, because coffee that is too wet can get mold during the trip. After that, we roast a small amount and do the cupping. We smell the coffee, and then we taste it with a spoon, very loudly. Every coffee gets a score. A lot that gets eighty points or more is specialty coffee, and the buyers who look for specialty pay a much better price. The hardest part of my job is to be consistent. The score that I give on Monday must be the same score that I would give on Friday.

First, the samples of green coffee arrive at the lab. Then the taster counts the defects and checks the moisture content. After that, the team does the cupping and gives the lot a score. A lot that scores eighty points or more is sold as specialty coffee. The price is the futures price plus a differential. Finally, the buyer fixes the price before the shipment.
